intro_en:
This segment of the Israel National Trail travels from Makhtesh Ramon to the Arava, without passing near a road, a settlement or even an electricity pole. Together with segment 45 of the Israel National Trail, this route offers a more powerful desert experience than any other section of the trail, with desert landscapes and desert wildlife, flora and geology.

 Mitzpe Ramon - Nahal Gevanim (43)
 Gev Holit - Sapir (45)
character_en: Several climbs, each with a descent on its other side... Sections of walking along narrow ridge lines. Walking alternately through narrow and wide wadis
pois_en: Har Saharonim. Sha'ar Ramon (Ramon Gate). Parsat Nekarot (the Nekarot Horseshoe). Karbolet Haririm. Nahal Gelad. Gev Holit
important_en: Access to the Gev Holit overnight campsite is by 4x4 vehicle. It is very important to arrange water caching.

There is no source of drinking water at the overnight campsite. Drinking water and an organised campsite are available at the Be'erot campsite, about 3 km along an easy road from the Nahal Gevanim campsite.
After floods, you may need to wade through water at Parsat Nekarot.
Mobile phone reception in the area is poor.
description_en:
From the overnight campsite at Nahal Gevanim we turn south along the oil pipeline route, with the black marking. We climb to the saddle through which the oil pipeline enters Makhtesh Ramon from the south.
From the saddle we climb left, eastwards, with the green marking, and ascend Har Saharonim. Har Saharonim is a section of the crater's southern wall. It has an elongated, narrow shape and the route runs along it, close to the ridge line, giving the feeling of walking along the top of a wall.
One can notice the characteristic tilt of the layers that make up the mountain. Looking left, into the crater, we see Givat Ga'ash, Ma'ale Mahmal, Har Ardon, and also the scar on the landscape made by the oil pipeline across the width of the crater, most conspicuously on its climb out of the crater near Ma'ale Mahmal.
At the point where the green trail turns left and descends to Ein Saharonim, the Israel National Trail continues with a black-marked trail along the ridge line and turns right, towards the descent to Nahal Ramon. At this point we can make out the skyline of Har Ardon, and in front of it, in one line, a green patch of vegetation and a dark conical hill. The green patch is Ein Saharonim, a small spring in Nahal Ramon surrounded by water-loving vegetation. The conical hill is indeed called Givat Harut (Cone Hill).
During the descent from Har Saharonim, we see ahead of us a layered wall, at the foot of which runs Nahal Ramon. This is 'Sha'ar Ramon' (Ramon Gate), the point where Nahal Ramon breaks out of the crater through the crater wall. Through the crater's gate flow the waters that Nahal Ramon drains from most of the crater's area, and with them stones, rocks and sand, products of erosion swept along by the water. On leaving the crater, Nahal Ramon flows into Nahal Nekarot, into which the runoff from the entire crater drains. On its way to the Arava, Nahal Nekarot also receives the streams Ardon, Haririm, Ma'ok and Kamai, which drain the rest of the crater (the Ardon Valley).
At the end of the descent from Har Saharonim, and after a short walk in Nahal Ramon in the direction of the water flow, we join the wide channel of Nahal Nekarot coming from the right. We continue down Nahal Nekarot to the left, towards 'Parsat Nekarot' (the Nekarot Horseshoe), together with a blue-marked trail. Parsat Nekarot is the name for a large meander made by Nahal Nekarot. Towards the completion of the meander, the Nekarot channel enters a short gorge, a narrow passage between pale rock walls. In rainy winters the pools inside the gorge fill with water and the passage through the gorge becomes a 'wet' one. The Israel National Trail bypasses the gorge to the south and ensures a comfortable, dry passage. On most days the passage through the gorge along the blue-marked trail will also be dry.
We pass a cave carved by floodwaters into the wall of the right bank, known as the Nekarot Cave. This is a shady and pleasant place to stop and rest. From here, it is a short walk to 'Mifar Nekarot' (the Nekarot Gap): the low hills to our left that form a gap, a break in the continuity of the crater's southern wall. The streams Ardon and Haririm, which drain the western part of the Ardon Valley, flow out of the crater here and drain into Nahal Nekarot.
At the confluence of the streams, Nahal Nekarot turns sharply south and enters a canyon. We pass a trail junction where a red-marked road coming from inside the crater (Ma'ale Dkalim) continues down Nahal Nekarot to the south. After the junction, the Israel National Trail continues a short distance east up Nahal Ardon, with a black-marked road. Ahead of us rises Karbolet Haririm (the Haririm Crest), a prominent peak with a jagged top.
The trail turns east with the blue marking, and passes a large acacia tree, a possible rest stop. From here the trail climbs up a channel that circles Karbolet Haririm from the south and east. The trail reaches a saddle and turns west, continuing to climb to the ridge line.
On the ridge line, the colourful and majestic view of the Ardon Valley and the eastern crater opens up before us. In the Ardon Valley one can make out straight dark lines, called dykes. This is magma that penetrated into cracks in the rock, cooled and solidified in a vertical form.
After the walk along the ridge line, the trail curves east, towards the descent in the direction of Nahal Ma'ok. Between the spur we descend and the ridge on the left (which has tilted layers) runs Nahal Ma'ok. Nahal Ma'ok leaves the crater through 'Mifar Ma'ok' (the Ma'ok Gap) and flows to Nahal Nekarot. At the end of the descent we reach the stream channel, where we can enjoy a break in the shade of one of the acacia trees.
Together with a tributary of Nahal Ma'ok, the trail climbs from the northern side of the stream to a saddle on the watershed between Nahal Ma'ok and Nahal Gelad. From the saddle we descend to Nahal Gelad, and bypass two waterfalls down the channel. After the second waterfall, near an acacia tree, it is worth stopping and looking back. On the wall of the channel, folded rock layers can be seen, resembling a slice of yeast cake. The dramatic geological events that occurred in Makhtesh Ramon and its surroundings created faults and folds that are revealed in this unique local phenomenon as well.
We continue walking down the channel to a nearby confluence of channels; it is recommended to turn left into a tributary of Nahal Gelad. Up the tributary, after a short walk, we reach Ein Gelad, a small spring, or more precisely a 'tamila', that is, a pocket of soil in the channel that holds water for a long period, where the water can be reached by digging in the ground. The tamila lies at the foot of a small waterfall, to the right of which grows an acacia tree; green vegetation at the foot of the waterfall indicates a moist area with a little water in the soil.
We retrace our steps to Nahal Gelad, and walk along the channel to the top of a large horseshoe shared by two waterfalls of two streams, Gelad and Kamai. The trail leads right to a descent through a hewn passage to the wide channel at the foot of the horseshoe.
A short spur of the trail with blue marking leads left to a pool at the foot of the Nahal Gelad waterfall, known as 'Gev Holit'. Holit is a former name of the stream, from before a change in which the names of other streams in the area were also updated. You can go to the pool and return by the same path. Opposite, we see the other waterfall, of Nahal Kamai, with several large boulders at its foot.
We walk down the wide channel of Nahal Kamai for a few minutes to the Gev Holit overnight campsite, which lies to the left of the confluence of Nahal Kamai with Nahal Nekarot.
author_en: Itzik Ben Dov, Trail Marking Coordinator, Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel (SPNI).
